title: Choose who, not just what.
description: You cannot decide every detail in advance when building something difficult. Jensen explains why choosing the people matters.

transcript: You gotta go through thick and thin.
There are a lot of unpredictable things in the future.
And it's because you're building a chip together. It's a foundry.
It's not exactly like buying something off the shelf.
You're building a chip together, and it's really hard to build chips.
So it's impossible to know all the details.
It's impossible to make all the decisions up front.
You really are choosing not...
what to buy, but who to work with.

reviewNote: The chip-building example explains the conclusion. A finished product can be specified in advance; a difficult collaboration keeps producing decisions that nobody could fully anticipate. Jensen is describing why a partner's judgment and values matter when the written plan runs out.

title: Why 74 days? Why not six?
description: Question the starting point before improving the process. A fresh analysis reveals what is possible and which tradeoffs explain the rest.

transcript: I don't like going into a problem, and somebody says,
It takes 74 days to do this today.
And we can do it for you in 72 days.
I'd rather strip it all back to zero
First of all, explain to me
why 74 days in the first place.
Let's think about what's possible today.
And if I were to build it completely from scratch,
How long would it take?
Oftentimes, you'd be surprised.
It might come to six days.
Now, the rest of the six days, the 74, could be
very well reasoned, and compromises,
cost reductions, and all kinds of different things.
But at least you know what they are.
Now that you know that six days is possible,
then the conversation from 74 to six,
surprisingly much more effective.

reviewNote: The six day result is a hypothetical example, not a measured productivity claim. The useful step is to separate physical possibilities from inherited assumptions, then identify which real costs and compromises explain the remaining time. The clip keeps that qualification.

title: Even Jensen gets nervous.
description: Asked about the whole world watching his keynote, Jensen admits he is always nervous because he wants to do a good job.

transcript: Were you nervous before the keynote?
The whole world watching.
I was super nervous, but I’m always nervous.
Every public speaking, doesn’t matter what it is.
Keeps you sharp?
Yeah, well, I don’t take it for granted.
I want to do a good job.
Because everything comes together at such a last moment,
it’s hard to practice at all, and we don’t.
And so I don’t know exactly
all the words that I’m gonna say.
And there’s no teleprompter.

reviewNote: Lex asks whether Jensen was nervous before the keynote. Jensen describes nerves as a recurring part of public speaking, then explains the last-minute nature of preparing this particular event. His comments about practice describe his process here, not a recommendation to avoid preparation.

title: Engineers deserve the spotlight.
description: Lex reflects on seeing an engineer welcomed like a rock star, and what that could mean for a young person choosing a path.

transcript: It’s really inspiring to see an engineer be treated like a rock star,
because engineers build the world,
and they don’t often get the love I think they deserve.
And you’re an inspiration to thousands,
millions of young kids who will be like, “Okay, I’m gonna...
I’m gonna be an engineer too.”
That’s right. Exactly.

reviewNote: After a crowded Computex visit, Lex tells Jensen why seeing an engineer treated like a rock star feels inspiring. Lex speaks most of this excerpt; Jensen agrees at the end. The text must not attribute Lex’s observation to Jensen or claim a measured effect on career choices.

title: Trust starts with honest limits.
description: Jensen recalls why Morris Chang stood out: clear limits, core values, integrity and a promise kept over decades.

transcript: People ask me, why did I end up choosing TSMC instead of UMC?
And the reason was because I like both companies equally.
They’re both excellent companies.
But the thing that I really liked about TSMC was,
there were a lot of things that I said that Morris said, “We can’t do that.”
And I’ll say, “What about that?” “We can’t do that.”
There’s a lot of things that they just can’t do.
And so he had a philosophy about his business,
and he has a set of core values that he cares about.
And he spent all his time talking about corporate governance
and integrity,
partnership and thinking long term.
And not once did he talk about anything else.
And he said one thing. He said,
“Jensen, if we were to work together,
I promise you we would jump through hoops for you.”
And for the whole time, 30 years, they’ve been jumping through hoops for us.
Yeah. He kept his word.
The core values of that company are really, really strong.
It was there from the very beginning.

reviewNote: Jensen recalls choosing between TSMC and UMC, says he liked both, and explains what stood out about Morris Chang. The honest-limits title is an editorial interpretation of the refusals, stated values and promise he describes. This passage preserves the comparison and reasoning; it is distinct from the earlier clip about choosing who to work with.

title: Never forget your roots.
description: A question about gamers brings Jensen back to where NVIDIA began and a reminder to keep his feet on the ground.

transcript: And you give some love to the gamers too, with the laptops and the games.
Oh, I love the gamers. That’s where we all begin.
You know, don’t forget your roots.
No matter how high you are,
don’t let your feet leave the ground.

reviewNote: During a Computex visit, Lex asks about showing love to gamers. Jensen connects the gaming community to NVIDIA’s beginnings, then offers a reminder about staying grounded. This is a personal reflection in the recording, not a complete company history.

title: Scarcity can spark invention.
description: Lex describes AI teams short of compute. Jensen points to the efficient architectures that constraints can encourage.

transcript: You know what all the AI companies are saying?
They’re compute starved.
More compute.
Yeah, but somehow, while they’re compute starved,
it forces them to come up with these
incredible architectures that are so efficient.
Constraints is the kind of mother of invention.
Right.
Scarcity.

reviewNote: Lex has been discussing visits to AI and robotics companies in China. They reflect on the pressure to find efficient architectures when compute is scarce. This is a conversational observation, not a benchmark, a claim about every AI company, or an endorsement of any particular restriction.

title: Nobody called back. Then Morris Chang did.
description: Repeated calls went unanswered. Jensen wrote a letter, and an unexpected call from Morris Chang brought new hope.

transcript: And I called several times. Nobody called me. Nobody called me back.
And so I finally wrote a letter to Morris.
I wrote a long letter and sent it to him.
Didn’t hear anything for a long time, and then one day,
it was around maybe 6:00 or so, maybe 6:30 or so.
This person calls and says, “This is Morris Chang from TSMC.”
Meanwhile, everybody outside my office was playing video games.
And they’re all laughing and screaming.
I think they were playing PlayStation, the first PlayStation at the time.
Everybody’s laughing and screaming. I said,
“Hey, guys, shut up. It’s Morris Chang.”
You know, called me back.
And so I was so happy
that a founder would actually call us back.
Because, hey, maybe we won’t have to die.

reviewNote: Jensen is recalling NVIDIA’s early search for a foundry. After unanswered calls to TSMC’s office, he wrote to Morris Chang, who later called him. The excerpt is his personal recollection, including the noisy office and relief; it does not establish a precise date or claim that one letter alone explains NVIDIA’s later success.

title: Goodwill is not a zero-sum game.
description: Success can grow through the people around you. Jensen and Lex discuss why wanting others to win creates more goodwill.

transcript: I like seeing other people succeed, even my colleagues in other companies.
It's a funny thing how the world works. If you just celebrate others
and you want them to succeed, somehow you succeed more.
For example, 43,000 employees at NVIDIA want me to succeed, literally.
You know what I’m saying?
And you want each of them to succeed.
Exactly.
I mean, I’ve seen you. You want people at other companies to succeed.
And they want me to succeed.
And there’s a ripple effect to the whole thing.
Yeah, exactly.
Goodwill is not a zero-sum game.
It’s not limited by physics.

reviewNote: Asked about the responsibility of fame, Jensen says he likes seeing other people succeed. The exchange expands from colleagues and employees to goodwill as something that can grow for everyone. The employee number is his statement in the recording, not a current headcount.

title: Fairness takes time.
description: A lasting partnership cannot anticipate every unknown. Jensen explains why fairness can balance out over time.

transcript: And the reason that it’s wisdom is, how do you capture in advance
all the unknowns in a relationship?
It’s like writing up
an ironclad prenup or something.
The problem is, the more specific you want it to become,
the more brittle that relationship is going to be.
And so I had the wisdom of keeping it nice and loose,
discover our way there. Rough justice.
We use this phrase, “rough justice.”
Sometimes they win, sometimes I win.
Sometimes I like how things worked out better than they did.
Sometimes they like it better than I did.
Over the course of time, it all works out.

reviewNote: Jensen has just described a decades-long relationship with TSMC. He argues that trying to specify every future contingency can make a relationship brittle, and describes fairness across repeated interactions. This is his partnership philosophy, not advice to abandon legal protections or accept lasting unfairness.

title: Even dinner has an objective function.
description: An empty plate can mean different things to different hosts. Jensen and Lex find an optimization problem hiding in a generous meal.

transcript: Depending on the culture, depending on the culture,
if you don’t eat everything, it’s rude.
And in some cultures, if you eat everything, it’s rude.
So you’re either competing for their generosity
or competing for your appreciation for their food.
And they’re both important, but depending on culture,
one’s more important than the other.
So in this culture, their generosity is more important
than your appreciation for the food.
That’s a kind of optimization problem.
Yeah. So you just gotta know which country you’re in.
You gotta figure out the objective function based on country.
That’s right. Conditional country.

reviewNote: After being given more food than they can finish, Jensen and Lex discuss how hospitality changes the meaning of an empty plate. Jensen’s cultural generalizations are part of a playful conversation, not universal etiquette rules. Lex supplies the objective-function punchline.

title: The kindness behind the street food
description: After a night market visit, Jensen notices the generosity of people who work hard and take pride in their craft.

transcript: Everybody's working hard for a living, and they're working so hard,
and they still want to share a little something with you.
They don't have that much money.
Their profit margin on that thing must be a dime each.
They gave me all their profit, right?
Just to be kind.
It's the Taiwanese way,
and it's nice to watch these people, their craft.

reviewNote: His attention shifts from the food to the people doing the work. The remark about a dime of profit is his estimate, not a verified margin. The moment is revealing because he notices the generosity of a small gesture as well as the skill behind it.

title: The beauty of imperfection
description: A spontaneous aside at Computex about learning to appreciate imperfection and the beauty of things that are one of a kind.

transcript: Look at that. That's beautiful.
When I was young, I would think that that's not good.
But now, I love wabi-sabi.
Beautiful things... imperfect.
I love that.
Imperfection is beauty.
Look at that. One of a kind.

reviewNote: This is a spontaneous reflection on how his taste has changed, rather than a formal design rule. He is responding to a display and appreciating something singular. The short exchange leaves room for imperfection without claiming to identify a particular defect.

title: First, breakfast. Then, TSMC.
description: Lex tries to return to the TSMC story. Jensen has a delicious reason to pause. A small, unguarded moment over breakfast.

transcript: You said you were looking for a foundry.
Just telling the story of how you
first returned back to Taiwan...
I see, I see.
...and built the relation with TSMC.
You know, Windows 95.
This is too important to me.
TSMC or that?
No, I can't talk.
Okay, yeah.
Priorities in life.
Lex, I will share this with you in a second,
but this is too important to me.
There we go.

reviewNote: The humor depends on the question and response staying together. Lex is trying to resume the TSMC story while Jensen enjoys his breakfast. It is a momentary, playful pause, not a statement that the food matters more than the relationship they are discussing.
